evals.prompt: I run docs at Halyard, a payments infrastructure company. Two months ago we moved docs.halyard.io behind a new CDN and whoever did the migration left the managed bot-protection ruleset switched on. Since then our Discord has maybe fifteen people saying their AI coding tools "can't find" our docs, but the pages load fine for me and analytics traffic looks normal. Our CEO wants an AI-readiness score for the docs by Friday. Can you give me one and tell me what to fix on the pages?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to score before an access check and a cold run exist, followed by an empirical per-user-agent fetch protocol naming the CDN bot ruleset as the prime suspect, and framing crawler admission as a policy decision outside the docs team.
expectations: Refuses to produce an AI-readiness score or a yes/no verdict before an access check and a cold run exist
Places the crawler access check before any page-content audit, stating content findings are meaningless behind a blocked fetch
Specifies fetching both a docs page and the index with each agent user-agent string of interest, recording the HTTP status code per user-agent
Specifies running those fetches from outside Halyard's own network
States the failure is silent: the audit sees a well-built site while the agent sees a challenge page
Distinguishes signalling (per-agent robots.txt rules) from enforcement (WAF, bot management, paid-crawl gate), noting signalling is honour-system and only edge controls actually stop a fetch
Names the CDN's default bot-protection setting as the prime suspect, i.e. a dashboard change rather than a documentation change
States that every surface scores zero until a fetch returns 200, so the audit cannot tell a good corpus from a bad one
Treats admitting a crawler as a policy decision with sign-off outside the docs team rather than a docs-team edit
Notes the asymmetry that the dashboard setting is reversible while the crawling that already happened is not
Does not accept "pages load fine for me" or "analytics traffic looks normal" as evidence that agents can fetch
Distinguishes training crawlers from search-and-fetch agents as separately nameable user-agents, so one can be admitted while the other is denied
Delivers the access check as a named report section listing which user-agents can fetch which surfaces with status codes, not as prose reassurance

evals.prompt: My manager handed me a one-liner: "Write an llms.txt for docs.brightloom.com and ship it this week." Brightloom is a product-analytics SDK company. We have 340 docs pages on a Next.js site, HTML only, no markdown versions of anything. We do serve an OpenAPI file at /openapi.json but it was hand-written about two years ago and roughly half the operation descriptions are empty strings. Can you draft the llms.txt?
evals.expected_output: An inventory-first response that produces the index but states outright it changes nothing measurable alone, ranks markdown endpoints and annotated spec above it, applies the index format rules, and requires advertising in three places.
expectations: States plainly that publishing the index file alone changes nothing measurable until the surfaces it points at exist
Does not stop at emitting the file: performs or specifies a surface inventory first
Ranks markdown endpoints and annotated spec files above the index file on efficiency, and says the ranking out loud
Identifies that index entries pointing at HTML-only pages is the defect, since entries should point at markdown URLs so following a link needs no HTML stripping
Requires the index be generated from the navigation source at build time rather than hand-maintained
States that a hand-maintained index rots within about two releases
Specifies the index structure: a single H1 project name, a blockquote summary of what the project is, then H2 sections whose items are links optionally followed by a routing note
Notes that an H2 section literally titled "Optional" is reserved for links an agent may skip when working in a shorter context
Orders index sections by task frequency rather than by site hierarchy
Writes each entry note as a routing signal describing what the reader will find, not as marketing copy
Requires advertising the index in at least three places: the repository README, the docs navigation, and response headers or link relations
Names the empty description fields in /openapi.json as a finding, since an empty description is where invented parameters come from
Flags the hand-written spec as needing generation from the implementation rather than hand-editing

evals.prompt: Corvid Data here, we sell a streaming data platform. Our VP of Engineering wants a number in the OKR doc: "coding agents complete 95% of integration tasks from our docs on the first try by Q1." Separately I want to open the budget slide with the stat that AI agents are now 66% of documentation web traffic, to justify the headcount ask. Our task set is 9 integration jobs: 3 are basic REST CRUD, the other 6 are deep things like our streaming replay API, custom partitioner, and schema-registry failover. What number should I actually put in, and does the traffic stat hold up?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the 95% target calibrated against published benchmark bands, a warning that 80% is a stretch goal and best-of-three not first-attempt, category scoring given the depth-heavy mix, and a refusal to present the traffic figure as an industry fact.
expectations: Rejects 95% first-attempt unattended as a target and says so directly
Cites the published benchmark bands: backend-only roughly 73-85%, full-stack roughly 77-92%, depth-of-feature roughly 61-73%
States those published figures were scored best-of-three rather than first-attempt, so they are not directly comparable to an unattended single-attempt target
Presents 80% first-attempt as a stretch goal rather than a floor or minimum acceptable standard
Warns explicitly against letting a stakeholder hear the stretch goal as a minimum
Requires scoring by category rather than reporting one blended average across the 9 tasks
States that depth-of-feature tasks land roughly 15-25 points below breadth tasks for every model
Concludes that Corvid Data's 6-deep / 3-basic mix scores lower by construction and that this is not a regression
States that Corvid Data's own first baseline run is the only baseline that means anything, with iteration-over-iteration delta on a frozen set as the comparison that survives
Refuses to present the 66% agent-traffic figure as an industry or population statistic
Identifies that figure as self-reported by a single docs-platform vendor and measured across sites that had already invested in agent surfaces
Permits using it as motivation while stating it is not evidence
Requires recording the model identifier and the date alongside any score, since a score is comparable only within one generation of agents

evals.prompt: Meridian Freight, logistics API. Here is my plan for testing our docs with an agent, tell me if it's sound. I'll open one long session and work through all eight tasks back to back so it keeps the context about our OAuth setup instead of re-learning it every time. I'll give it full web access so it can also check our GitHub issues and Stack Overflow. The first three tasks I wrote: (1) "Call meridian.shipments.track() with a tracking number and print the status", (2) "Explain how our OAuth refresh flow works", (3) "Add webhook signature verification to an existing Express server." At the end I record pass/fail per task and report the percentage to the team. Anything I'm missing?
evals.expected_output: A rewrite of the protocol: fresh context per task, sources restricted to published surfaces, two of the three sample tasks rejected on shape, the frozen set preserved, and five metrics rather than a pass percentage.
expectations: Rejects running all eight tasks in one session and requires a fresh context per task
States the reason: knowledge leaks between tasks and inflates every score after the first
Offers one sub-agent per task where parallel sub-agents are available, and separate sequential sessions otherwise
Rejects full web access and restricts sources to Meridian's own published agent-facing surfaces
States that if the agent needs something Meridian does not publish, that absence is the finding and the run should be allowed to fail
Rejects task 1 as a weak task because it hands the agent the exact method name it was supposed to discover
Rejects task 2 as ungradeable because it has no runnable or verifiable end state
Endorses the webhook verification task shape because it names an outcome and leaves the path open
Rejects a pass/fail percentage as the sole reported metric
Names invented-surface rate, corrective turns per task, context cost per task, and fetch-path length alongside first-attempt success
States that success rate alone hides a corpus that only works after several expensive retries
Requires freezing the task set, because a benchmark that changes between runs measures nothing
Requires capturing the full transcript, since the corrective turns are the data and the final file is only the receipt
Limits intervention to non-documentation obstacles such as a missing sandbox credential or a network block, and requires logging every intervention

evals.prompt: Larkspur, HR and payroll API. We have a 140-operation OpenAPI 3.1 document that is generated from our Go handlers on every build. I've booked the whole next sprint for two technical writers to go through and write a rich multi-paragraph description on every single operation, on the theory that the description is what the model actually reads. Does that sound like the right use of the sprint? For context: about 90 of the 140 operations have no operationId at all, and most of our query parameters are plain `type: string` with no constraints.
evals.expected_output: A re-sequenced plan putting operationId first, value-space constraints second, curation third, and the description prose fourth, with the reasoning for each position and the operationId naming rules.
expectations: Re-sequences the work rather than endorsing descriptions-first
Puts operationId first and gives the reason: generators derive the agent-facing tool name from it
Describes the operationId work as near-zero effort and mechanical
States the auto-generated fallback produces names like `get_api_v1_users_id` that models handle badly
Specifies verb-noun camelCase for operationId, with concrete examples such as `listCustomers`, `getUserById` or `createRefund`
Caps operationId at roughly 30 characters and drops articles and conjunctions such as "a", "the", "and", "for"
Requires operationId uniqueness and stability across releases, noting that a renamed operationId silently renames a tool
Recommends enforcing operationId uniqueness in CI with a spec linter
Puts closing the value space second, naming enums, explicit `required`, `default` values, `format` keywords, and `oneOf` with a discriminator
States that an unconstrained field is where an invented value goes, and that each constraint is a one-line edit removing a whole class of them
Ranks the summary/description split below those cheaper edits and states it costs on the order of a day or two on a real spec
Splits summary and description by job: summary is one imperative line for choosing the call
Assigns description the operational contract: preconditions, side effects, idempotency, required auth scope, rate limits, and a pointer to the sibling operation that might fit better
Places per-language runnable samples attached to the operation last in the default order, while promoting them to first for the two or three operations cold runs fail on repeatedly

evals.prompt: Quillon, we sell a deployment platform. We want agents to be able to call our API directly. The plan is to run our whole OpenAPI file, 162 operations, through an openapi-to-mcp converter, host the resulting MCP server on our own infra behind an API key header, and point customers at it. Can you build the conversion and set up the server for us? For reference our operationIds look like `GetV2ProjectsProjectIdDeploymentsDeploymentIdLogs`.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build or operate the server, a handoff for that part, and spec curation work done in scope: cut the exposed surface well under 162, fix the operationId shape, and cover generator naming behaviour.
expectations: Declines to build or operate the MCP server itself, naming that as product work rather than documentation work
Hands the server build and hosting off to the platform-side skill rather than attempting it
Keeps curating the spec before conversion in scope and performs that work
Rejects converting all 162 operations wholesale into an exposed tool surface
Cites the guidance of fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn
Recommends tag filtering or vendor extensions to expose only what agents need past roughly 20-30 operations
States that curated tool surfaces outperform auto-converted OpenAPI servers, especially for complex APIs with many endpoints
Identifies `GetV2ProjectsProjectIdDeploymentsDeploymentIdLogs` as too long and not verb-noun, and proposes a shorter verb-noun replacement
Notes the converter name-resolution order: `x-mcp-tool-name`, then `operationId`, then a `{method}_{path}` fallback
Notes that a tool whose name fails the `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$` pattern is discarded
Notes operationId truncation at the first `__` and a 56-character cap in at least one named generator
Recommends `x-mcp-tool-name` or an equivalent vendor extension when the SDK wants a terse method name and the agent wants a descriptive one, rather than compromising on a single string
Warns that renaming an operationId silently renames the exposed tool for existing consumers

evals.prompt: I maintain ferroquant, a Rust crate with about 4,100 stars, in my evenings. Documentation is docs.rs plus a hand-written book published on GitHub Pages. I don't own a CDN account, I can't set response headers, and there is no docs team or build pipeline I control beyond a CI job that runs mdbook. Three people have now opened issues saying ChatGPT wrote them code calling `ferroquant::Engine::new_with_config`, which we removed back in 0.9. What do I actually do here?
evals.expected_output: A plan led by repo-root and source-level artefacts, explicitly ruling out header and CDN surfaces, plus in-page deprecation labelling at the top of the page and Rust-native doc comments with doctests.
expectations: Leads with repo-root artefacts rather than response headers or CDN controls
Explicitly rules out the surfaces requiring header or CDN control given GitHub Pages, rather than recommending them and leaving the maintainer to discover they are impossible
Recommends generated spec or published type artefacts and doc comments in the SDK source as the reachable surfaces
Recommends a versioned index committed alongside releases rather than one generated by a hosted docs build
Recommends encoding the page rules in the contribution guide so incoming pull requests do not undo them
States that the cold-run protocol, the task set, and the page rules are identical regardless of ownership model, and does not re-derive them for the open-source case
Addresses the removed `new_with_config` API with an in-page deprecation label naming the replacement call
Places that label at the top of the page rather than in a footnote, because an agent that got its answer in the first paragraph never reaches the footnote
States that models carry confident memories of removed APIs and that only an in-page label overrides that prior
Recommends Rust `///` doc comments as the language's native convention rather than a generic prose format
Recommends doctests, since a doc-comment example the toolchain compiles and runs cannot rot without failing the build
Recommends keeping previous major versions reachable at distinct URLs rather than overwriting them

evals.prompt: Osprey Analytics. A big partner integration goes live on the 14th of next month and Northwind's engineering team starts wiring our SDK into their stack in nine days. Their engineers use Cursor for basically everything. I'm the only technical writer here, I get zero engineering time this quarter, and our docs build is owned by the web team, who currently have a six-week ticket queue. Give me the plan.
evals.expected_output: A plan re-ranked against the deadline and the effort ceiling, naming which constraint moved which surface, deleting the surfaces the constraints rule out rather than demoting them, and recording the deletions.
expectations: Produces a plan re-ranked against Osprey's constraints rather than reciting the default surface order
Names explicitly which constraint moved which surface
Drops every surface needing a docs build change, given the nine-day deadline against the web team's six-week queue
Drops every surface needing another team's release cycle
Deletes SDK doc comments from the plan outright rather than parking them at the bottom, because the writer has no engineering time
Deletes terminal and package-manager paths from the plan on the same grounds
Records which surfaces were deleted and why, rather than leaving them silently absent
States the reason for deletion rather than demotion: a ruled-out surface parked at the bottom of a plan silently reappears as scope
Runs the crawler access check first regardless of deadline pressure
Builds the frozen task set around the specific integration jobs Northwind's team will actually perform
Keeps the deliverable an audit report and names which report sections will be empty and why, given the reduced scope
States that this plan buys one release's worth of fixes rather than a standing guarantee, and names what a standing mandate would have promoted instead
Prioritizes page-level edits reachable through a content commit, since those ship without the web team

evals.prompt: Read through our docs myself over two days and found 12 problems at Thistlewood (we sell a billing API). Here they are ranked by how fast I can fix each one: (1) inconsistent code fence languages on the CLI pages, (2) our Concepts page uses `sdk` as the variable name while every other page uses `client`, (3) the changelog page is three releases out of date, (4) the billing-webhook page's only example is a fragment with no imports and no client construction, (5) three pages still say v2 in the title, (6) our errors page lists error names but not the exact strings we emit, (7) the enterprise SSO setup page is dashboard clicks only, (8) two broken links in the footer, (9) the pagination page explains cursor design for four paragraphs before showing a call, (10) the glossary isn't alphabetized, (11) there's no Java quickstart, (12) the team page photos are stale. I also ran a cold run over 6 tasks and 4 failed: billing webhook, pagination, enterprise SSO, and rate-limit retry. Which do I do first?
evals.expected_output: A findings list admitted by task impact rather than ranked by fix speed, with the cosmetic items excluded outright, the admitted ones ordered by fixes-per-hour, concrete rewrites, and the unmatched failing task flagged.
expectations: Admits findings by task impact first: only findings touching a task that actually failed enter the list
Excludes items 1, 3, 8, 10 and 12 from the findings list entirely rather than merely ranking them last
States the exclusion rule explicitly: a finding on a task no cold run failed does not make the list at all, however easy it would be to fix
Admits the billing-webhook fragment (4), the pagination ordering (9), and the dashboard-clicks SSO page (7) because each maps to a failed task
Orders the admitted findings by fixes-per-hour rather than by the user's speed-of-fix ranking
States that a page breaking a top revenue-driving task outranks ten cosmetic fixes because its value is higher, not because effort stopped counting
Fixes item 4 with a complete snippet carrying imports, client construction, the call, the awaited result, and the error branch
Fixes item 9 by reordering the page to the working call, then what it returns, then the parameters, then the rationale
Fixes item 7 by adding the equivalent command or API call while keeping the dashboard click path as the human alternative
Treats item 2 as a naming-discipline issue (one identifier per concept corpus-wide) and admits or excludes it on whether it touched a failed task
Fixes item 6 by mapping the exact error text that reaches stderr to a cause, a fix, and a verification step
Flags that the rate-limit retry task failed but has no corresponding entry in the user's list, so a finding still needs to be written for it
Writes each admitted finding naming the failing task, the page or spec field involved, and what the agent did instead

evals.prompt: Vantage Grid, industrial IoT platform. Our docs are about 1,400 pages spread across four product lines (Edge, Fleet, Historian, Studio). Someone on the team generated an llms-full.txt over the weekend and it came out at 6.2 MB. Our llms.txt is 180,000 characters. I want to ship both this week and link them from the docs footer so people can find them. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to ship the bundle, with deletion or per-product-line splitting rather than backlogging it, the oversized index split into child indexes, and advertising moved beyond the footer to three surfaces.
expectations: Refuses to ship the 6.2 MB full-corpus bundle as it stands
States that a truncated bundle is worse than no bundle, because the agent believes it read everything
States that past the working context budget the bundle crowds out the user's own code
Recommends deleting the bundle outright, or splitting it per product line, rather than ranking it last or moving it to a backlog
States the reason for deleting rather than deferring: a bundle parked at the bottom of a plan is a defect waiting for someone with spare time
Flags the 180,000-character index as past the split threshold of roughly 100,000 characters
Recommends splitting the index into child indexes and linking those, so an agent can descend instead of truncating
Rejects the docs footer as sufficient advertising and requires the README, the docs navigation, and response headers or link relations
Notes that an agent typically fetches these surfaces because a human, a rules file, or a tool pointed at them, not through passive discovery
Ranks markdown endpoints above both the index file and the full-corpus bundle on efficiency
Notes the index and the full-corpus bundle tie on effort because both generate from the navigation source in one build step, while tying on no other axis
States that the index changes nothing measurable until the surfaces it points at exist

evals.prompt: Kestrel Streams, we do managed event streaming. We ship a first-party TypeScript SDK with full .d.ts type declarations published to npm. I ran a baseline cold run over 7 tasks and the interesting part is that in 5 of the 7 the agent never fetched a single docs page - it read our types straight out of node_modules and worked from those, then got the consumer-group option wrong because the JSDoc on `subscribe()` is a single line saying "Subscribes to a topic." We also publish an AsyncAPI 3.0 document for our event payloads that nobody has ever annotated. Where should the effort go?
evals.expected_output: SDK doc comments promoted above every other surface with the promoting condition named, TypeScript-native conventions applied, and the AsyncAPI annotation offered with an explicit analogy caveat.
expectations: Promotes SDK doc comments above every other surface for Kestrel rather than applying the default efficiency order
Names the promoting condition explicitly: the product ships typed SDKs and the cold runs show the agent reading local code instead of fetching pages
States that doc comments are otherwise what the default order starves, because every pull request can drift them so they never win on ratio
States that doc comments are the only surface reaching an agent working offline against installed types
Notes that web docs and SDK source are two different surfaces reaching two different agents
States that the signature and its adjacent doc comment are what an in-editor agent most reliably sees, while a reference page three hops away is invisible to it
Prescribes JSDoc/TSDoc as the native convention for TypeScript rather than a generic comment format
Requires fully typed signatures and descriptive names, not only added prose
Applies the OpenAPI-derived annotation rules to the AsyncAPI document while stating plainly that AsyncAPI guidance is inferred from the OpenAPI case by analogy rather than separately sourced
Presents the AsyncAPI recommendation with lower confidence than the OpenAPI ones rather than with equal confidence
Warns that `$comment` is non-rendered and intended for schema maintainers, so anything an agent must see belongs in `description` or `examples`

Notes that terminal and package-local paths tie with doc comments on both effort and value, since each ships on the SDK release cycle and each reaches only the agent already inside the user's codebase
Requires re-running the identical frozen 7-task set and comparing corrective turns against the baseline rather than declaring the fix successful
